I came into software from healthcare, and the habits stuck: rigid protocols, zero tolerance for error, and a reflex for the edge cases nobody thought to check. Today I build products that run in production — from a medical platform published on the app stores to a coupon aggregator I maintain on my own.

caseStudies.subtitle: Some builds, told the way I think about them — problem, approach, result.

items.problem: The Brazilian coupon market is full of slow, stale-data sites — there was no platform with real affiliate sync, smart search and alerts that fire before deals expire.
items.approach: Built a full-stack system with 5 affiliate sources via Adapter Pattern, BullMQ queues syncing every 3h, Meilisearch full-text search, double opt-in alerts and algorithmic scoring 0–100 by discount and expiry. Refactored an N+1 that locked up the database under load (thousands of individual upserts per cycle) into batched upserts deduplicated by (source, externalId), and alert matching went from N queries per coupon to 3 batched calls per cycle, regardless of volume.
items.result: A live platform with automatic sync of thousands of coupons, O(1) DB roundtrips for alert matching, 3-level threaded comments and a complete admin panel for coupons, stores and users.

items.problem: A real-money game in real time carries two risks: the player has no way to trust the outcome wasn't manipulated, and any balance inconsistency between services turns into loss.
items.approach: Game Service and Wallet Service communicate exclusively over RabbitMQ, with no direct HTTP — the Wallet is the single source of truth for balance, and partial failures don't create inconsistency. Four-layer DDD architecture keeping the domain layer in plain TypeScript (zero NestJS, zero Prisma) so business rules are testable without framework mocks. Monetary values as BigInt in cents, eliminating floating-point error.
items.result: 91 unit tests and 11 E2E scenarios covering bet → cashout → balance and bet → crash → loss. Every round is verifiable by the player via HMAC-SHA256: the seed hash is published before bets and revealed after the crash, so the crash point can be recomputed independently.

items.problem: Selling to Brazil and Europe from the same system means dealing with different currencies, taxes, payment gateways, and suppliers. International gateways break conversion at Brazilian checkout, and suppliers serving Portugal don't serve São Paulo. The obvious alternative — two separate systems — would duplicate catalog, orders, and maintenance.
items.approach: A single system with the differences isolated to specific points. Go backend running serverless on AWS Lambda, with one Supplier interface implemented by BR and EU providers — adding a supplier or a market doesn't change the order flow. The pricing pipeline computes local currency, margin, and destination-country tax (VAT) in isolated stages, and checkout uses MercadoPago (Pix, Boleto, card) in Brazil and Stripe/PayPal in Europe.
items.result: Two versions of the same product sharing one architecture: the European one, public, and the Brazilian one, adapted for BRL, local tax rules, and local payment methods. OAuth2/OIDC authentication with PKCE (Google, Facebook, Apple), parallel catalog sync via goroutines, and a streaming AI shopping assistant — working around API Gateway's 29-second connection ceiling with an explicit 28-second timeout.
items.links_note: The live site is the Brazilian version; the public code is the European one, which served as the base for the adaptation. The BR repository is private — available on request.

commandPalette.nav_services: What I bring to a team

diagram.caption: Hover a node (or tap it on mobile) to see what it is responsible for.

roles.web: Next.js 15 front end with SSR and ISR — coupon pages render on the server so Google can index them and they load fast.
roles.sources: Five different affiliate networks behind a single interface. Adding a sixth source doesn't touch the rest of the system.
roles.api: Fastify API: exposes search, alerts and the admin panel, and owns the coupon scoring rules.
roles.queue: Runs the sync every 3h outside the request cycle, writing in batches deduplicated by (source, externalId).
roles.search: Typo-tolerant full-text search — kept separate from Postgres so the two don't compete for connections.
roles.db: Source of truth: coupons, stores, users, alerts and 3-level threaded comments.
roles.cache: Caches hot listings and backs the queue.

diagram.caption: The central decision is RabbitMQ: Game and Wallet never talk to each other over HTTP.

roles.client: React client: everything goes through the gateway except the game itself — the multiplier curve arrives over WebSocket.
roles.keycloak: Issues and validates OAuth2/OIDC tokens. No service rolls its own authentication.
roles.kong: Front door: routes, validates the token and rate-limits before any request reaches a service.
roles.game: Runs the rounds and the provably fair algorithm. Four DDD layers with the domain in plain TypeScript — no NestJS and no Prisma inside the business rules.
roles.bus: All traffic between Game and Wallet goes through here. With no direct HTTP between services, a partial failure becomes a pending message rather than an inconsistent balance.
roles.wallet: The single source of truth for balance. Money as BigInt cents, with no floating point anywhere.
roles.db: Wallet persistence: bets, cashouts and the transaction history.

diagram.caption: One backend serves two markets — what changes per region is supplier, tax and gateway.

roles.web: Next.js 15 storefront with i18n in 7 languages and prices already converted to the visitor's currency.
roles.gw: API Gateway with an explicit 28s timeout, just under the 29s connection limit — that's what lets the AI assistant stream its answer without being cut off.
roles.api: Go backend running serverless. Owns the per-region pricing pipeline: local currency, margin and tax by destination country.
roles.mongo: Catalog, orders and sessions. Catalog sync runs in parallel via goroutines.
roles.br: Brazilian suppliers behind the Supplier interface — the same one the European ones implement.
roles.eu: European suppliers. Adding a new one doesn't change the order flow.
roles.pay: MercadoPago (Pix, Boleto, card) in Brazil; Stripe and PayPal in Europe. Routing is by destination country.

items.summary: Multi-market e-commerce platform for Brazil and the European Union, with international suppliers, geographic order routing, region-aware pricing, and an AI shopping assistant. The European version is public; the Brazilian adaptation runs in a private repository.
